position: end — after the verb and its object (*She speaks French well*); before its word as a degree adverb (*well over*, *well aware*); mid after *may*, *might*, *could* and *can* (*You may well be right*)
modifies: verbs; as a degree word, prepositions, adverbs, numbers and a few adjectives (*well after*, *well worth*)
form: suppletive — the adverb of the adjective *good*
contrast: *Good* is the adjective, *well* the adverb: *She's a good singer* / *She sings well* — *She sings good* is heard in casual American speech but is marked as wrong in careful English. *I'm well* (healthy) is the adjective, and *Well, I don't know* is the interjection; neither is this adverb. *As well* goes at the end of the clause (*I'll have a coffee as well*), not in the middle like Russian *тоже*. Before a past participle *well* makes a compound adjective that is hyphenated before a noun: *a well-known writer*, but *The writer is well known*.

senses.gloss: In a good, skillful or successful way.
examples: She speaks Spanish really *well*.
The interview went *well*, I think.
He plays guitar *better* than anyone else in the band.

senses.gloss: as well: also; too.
examples: I'd like a side salad *as well*.
She's a singer, and she writes her own songs *as well*.

senses.gloss: Thoroughly and carefully; completely.
examples: Shake *well* before using.
I don't know him very *well*.
Make sure you dry your hair *well* before you go out.

senses.gloss: By a large amount; far — before prepositions, adverbs and numbers.
examples: The party went on *well* after midnight.
The repairs cost *well* over $2,000.
Stand *well* back from the grill.

senses.gloss: Fully; quite — with *aware* and *worth*, and after *can* or *could* with *imagine*, *believe* or *afford*.
examples: I'm *well* aware of the risks.
The museum is *well* worth a visit.
I can *well* imagine how upset she was.

senses.gloss: Quite possibly; very likely — after *may*, *might* and *could*.
examples: You may *well* be right.
It could *well* rain tomorrow, so bring a jacket.

senses.gloss: might as well, may as well: there is no good reason not to; it would be just as good to.
examples: There's nothing on TV, so we *might as well* go to bed.
You *may as well* take the umbrella — it's by the door anyway.

senses.gloss: Kindly or with approval.
examples: Everyone at the office speaks *well* of her.
They treated us very *well* at the hotel.

senses.gloss: With enough money; in comfort.
examples: They live *well* on two teachers' salaries.
The job doesn't pay *well*, but I love it.

senses.gloss: Reasonably or properly — in *can't very well*, meaning that it would be wrong or awkward to do something.
examples: I can't very *well* say no to my own sister.
We couldn't very *well* leave before the speeches were over.

senses.gloss: Wisely — in *would do well to*.
examples: You would do *well* to listen to her advice.
New drivers would do *well* to stay off the highway at rush hour.

position: end — after the verb and its object (*He sang badly*); mid with *need*, *want* and before past participles (*I badly need*, *badly damaged*)
contrast: *Bad* is the adjective: *I feel bad* (sorry, guilty or sick) is the standard form, and *I feel badly* is common in American speech but often corrected. In casual American English *bad* also stands in for *badly* in the 'very much' sense (*I want it so bad*) — normal to hear, but avoid it in writing. When the meaning is 'less well', the comparative is *worse*, never *more badly*. Russian *мне плохо* is *I feel sick* or *I don't feel well*, not *I feel badly*.

senses.gloss: In a poor, unskillful or unsuccessful way.
examples: I did *badly* on the chemistry test.
The negotiations went *badly* from the start.
Our team played even *worse* in the second half.

senses.gloss: Seriously; causing a lot of harm or damage.
examples: Two people were *badly* hurt in the crash.
The roof was *badly* damaged by the storm.
The towns *worst* hit by the flooding are still without power.

senses.gloss: Very much — with *need*, *want* and *miss*.
examples: The house *badly* needs a coat of paint.
She wanted that job so *badly*.

senses.gloss: Unkindly, unfairly or in a way that is not acceptable.
examples: The company treated its workers *badly*.
The kids behaved *badly* at the restaurant.
Please don't think *badly* of me.

position: end — after the verb and its object (*I don't like it much*); before its word with comparatives and *too* (*much bigger*, *much too big*); mid with *prefer*, *appreciate* and *enjoy* (*I much prefer tea*)
modifies: verbs, comparatives, *too*, past participles and *the same*
contrast: Bare *much* after a verb in an affirmative statement sounds wrong: say *I like it a lot* or *I like it very much*, not *I like it much* — but *much* is natural in questions and negatives (*Do you like it much?*, *I don't like it much*). *Much* goes before comparatives and *very* before plain adjectives: *much bigger*, *very big*, never *very bigger*. Russian *много* after a verb is *a lot* in speech (*He works a lot*), and *гораздо* or *намного* is *much* or *a lot* before a comparative. *Much* before a noun (*much money*) is the determiner and belongs to that dictionary.

senses.gloss: To a great degree; a lot — mostly in questions and negatives, after *very* and *so*, and before past participles.
examples: I don't like horror movies *much*.
Thank you so *much* for coming.
Your help is very *much* appreciated.

senses.gloss: Far; a lot — before comparatives, *too* and *different*.
examples: The new apartment is *much* bigger than the old one.
This coffee is *much* too sweet.
The new phone isn't *much* different from the old one.

senses.gloss: Often; a lot of the time — in questions and negatives.
examples: Do you get out *much*?
We don't eat out *much* anymore.
We travel *more* now that the kids are grown.

senses.gloss: Nearly; about — in *much the same* and *pretty much*.
examples: The town looks *much* the same as it did twenty years ago.
That's *pretty much* all I know about it.

senses.gloss: not so much ... as: not really one thing but rather another — correcting how something is described.
examples: It's *not so much* the money — it's the principle.
He's *not so much* lazy as bored at school.
The problem wasn't *so much* the price as the delivery time.

senses.gloss: much less: and certainly not; let alone — after a negative.
senses.ru: не говоря уже о, тем более не
examples: He can't boil an egg, *much less* cook a whole dinner.
I've never even met her, *much less* gone out with her.

position: before its word — in *a little* before adjectives, adverbs and comparatives (*a little tired*); end after the verb (*She slept little*); front with inversion in *Little did I know*
modifies: verbs, adjectives, adverbs and comparatives (*a little faster*)
contrast: *A little* and bare *little* point in opposite directions: *I slept a little* (немного — I did get some sleep) vs *I slept little* (мало — not enough). In everyday American speech bare *little* sounds formal, and people say *not much* instead (*I didn't sleep much*). When *little* opens a clause it means 'not at all' and needs question word order: *Little did we know*, never *Little we knew*. The comparative is *less*, *least*; *littler* and *littlest* exist only for the adjective meaning small (*my littlest sister*), which belongs to the adjective dictionary.

senses.gloss: a little: to a small degree; slightly.
examples: I'm *a little* tired tonight.
Could you turn the music down *a little*?
Drive *a little* slower through the school zone.

senses.gloss: Not much; hardly at all — without *a*, often after *very*.
examples: The neighborhood has changed very *little*.
He ate *little* and said even *less*.
We see them very *little* these days.

senses.gloss: Not at all — before *know*, *think*, *realize* and *suspect*, usually at the front with inversion.
examples: *Little* did I know that she was going to be my new boss.
*Little* did they realize how much the trip would cost.

senses.gloss: little by little: gradually; a bit at a time.
examples: *Little by little*, the town recovered from the flood.
She paid off the loan *little by little*.

position: end — after the verb and its object (*She sings better*); mid in *had better* (*You'd better go*) and before a past participle (*better known*)
contrast: *Had better* is not a past tense and takes the bare verb: *You'd better go*, never *You'd better to go* or *You had better went*; the negative is *You'd better not*. It is stronger than *should* and can sound like a warning, so it is odd when advising a boss or a stranger. In casual American speech the *had* often drops out (*You better call her*), but keep it in writing. Russian *лучше* in a preference or suggestion is *I'd rather* or *let's*, not *better*: *Лучше я пойду пешком* is *I'd rather walk*. Americans often say *I like the blue one better* where British speakers tend to say *more*. *I feel better* (healthier) is the adjective.

senses.gloss: In a more skillful, successful or satisfactory way — the comparative of *well*.
examples: She speaks French *better* than I do.
The second interview went much *better*.
Things are going *better* at work now.

senses.gloss: More; to a greater degree — with *like*, *know* and *understand*, before past participles, and informally in *better than* before a number.
examples: Which do you like *better*, the mountains or the beach?
He's *better* known as a painter than as a writer.
The drive took *better* than three hours.

senses.gloss: had better: ought to; should — often as a warning.
examples: You'd *better* take an umbrella.
We *had better* leave before the traffic gets bad.
You *better* not tell Mom about this.

senses.gloss: know better: to be old enough or wise enough not to do something.
examples: You're twenty years old — you should *know better*.
She *knew better* than to argue with her father.

senses.gloss: think better of: to decide not to do something after thinking about it again.
examples: He opened his mouth to argue, then *thought better* of it.
I almost sent the angry email, but I *thought better* of it.

senses.gloss: better yet, better still: an even better idea is.
examples: Call her tonight — or *better yet*, go see her.
Text me when you land, or *better still*, just come straight over.

position: end — after the verb and its object (*She sings best*); before its word with past participles (*best known*)
contrast: After a verb, American English uses *best* with or without *the*: *Which song do you like best?* and *Which song do you like the best?* are both normal. Before a noun, *best* is the adjective (*my best friend*) and belongs to that dictionary. *At best* (в лучшем случае) is not *at its best* (в лучшей форме): *The team was at its best in the final*. *Had best* (*You had best leave*) is an old-fashioned or regional form of *had better*.

senses.gloss: In the most skillful, successful or satisfactory way — the superlative of *well*.
examples: She works *best* under pressure.
Which of the three cars handled *best* in the snow?
We fixed the fence as *best* we could.

senses.gloss: Most; to the greatest degree — with *like* and *know*, and before past participles.
examples: What did you like *best* about Chicago?
He's *best* known for his early films.
You know her *best* — what should I get her for her birthday?

senses.gloss: In the most suitable or sensible way — before past participles such as *done*, *left* and *avoided*.
examples: Some things are *best* left unsaid.
Pie dough is *best* made the day before.
Downtown is *best* avoided during rush hour.

senses.gloss: at best: even in the most favorable view — used to show that something is small, poor or limited.
examples: The plan will save us fifty dollars *at best*.
His Spanish is basic *at best*.
We'll finish in June *at best*, and more likely July.

position: end — after the verb and its object (*He played worse*); front as a linker (*Worse, nobody told us*)
form: suppletive — the comparative of *badly* and of the adjective *bad*
contrast: Never *badder* or *more bad*: *She did worse than last time*. Do not mix up *worse* (the comparative, used with *than*) and *worst* (the superlative, used with *the* or *of all*). *The weather is worse today* is the adjective. In casual American English *worse* also means 'more badly' with *want* and *need* (*I want it worse than you do*) — fine in speech, not in writing.

senses.gloss: In a poorer or less successful way; less well.
examples: I did *worse* on the final than on the midterm.
The team played even *worse* after halftime.
Things turned out *worse* than we expected.

senses.gloss: More severely or seriously; to a greater degree.
examples: My knee hurts *worse* today.
The Gulf Coast was hit *worse* than anyone expected.
Nobody wants this job *worse* than I do.

senses.gloss: worse, worse still, even worse: and what is more serious — adding a further bad fact.
examples: We missed the train, and *worse still*, it was the last one that night.
The company lost money. *Worse*, it hid the losses from investors.

position: end — after the verb (*Who played worst?*); before its word with past participles (*worst affected*); front in *worst of all* and *at worst*
modifies: verbs, past participles and whole clauses
form: suppletive — the superlative of *badly* and of the adjective *bad*
contrast: American English says *if worse comes to worst* (на худой конец), and many Americans also say *if worst comes to worst*; British English says *if the worst comes to the worst*. *The worst* before a noun or after *be* (*the worst day*, *That was the worst*) is the adjective and belongs to that dictionary.

senses.gloss: In the poorest or least successful way.
examples: Of all the kids in the class, I did *worst* in math.
The players who performed *worst* in camp were cut from the team.

senses.gloss: Most severely or seriously — often before past participles such as *hit* and *affected*.
examples: The coastal towns were *worst* hit by the hurricane.
Older patients were the ones *worst* affected by the virus.

senses.gloss: worst of all: and the most serious thing is.
examples: The food was cold, the service was slow, and *worst of all*, they overcharged us.
*Worst of all*, I lost every photo from the trip.

senses.gloss: at worst: if the worst happens; in the least favorable view.
examples: *At worst*, we'll have to pay a small late fee.
The mistake was careless *at worst* — nobody thinks it was dishonest.

position: before its word — before adjectives and adverbs (*more careful*); end after the verb (*You should sleep more*)
contrast: Short adjectives and adverbs take *-er*, not *more*: *faster*, *harder*, never *more fast* — and never both at once (*more better*, *more easier*). Russian *больше не* is *not anymore* or *no longer*, never *more not*: *Он здесь больше не живёт* is *He doesn't live here anymore*; American English writes *anymore* as one word in that sense. Russian *ещё* is *more* after a number (*once more*, *two more times*), but *ещё не* is *not yet*, *всё ещё* is *still*, and *ещё* before a comparative is *even* (*even bigger*), never *more bigger*. *More* before a noun (*more time*) is the determiner and belongs to that dictionary.

senses.gloss: Used before adjectives and adverbs to form the comparative.
examples: The second test was *more* difficult than the first.
Could you speak *more* slowly, please?
Flights are getting *more and more* expensive.

senses.gloss: To a greater degree or extent — with verbs.
examples: You need to sleep *more*.
I like him *more* every time I see him.
The *more* you practice, the easier it gets.

senses.gloss: Again; in addition — in *once more*, *twice more* and similar phrases.
examples: Let's try it once *more*.
The phone rang twice *more* before anyone picked up.

senses.gloss: more or less: approximately; almost.
examples: The kitchen is *more or less* finished.
It'll cost about three hundred dollars, *more or less*.

senses.gloss: Rather; more accurately — in *more ... than*, comparing two descriptions of the same thing.
examples: She was *more* surprised than angry.
He's *more* shy than rude — give him time.
For us, the trip was *more* about family than sightseeing.

senses.gloss: more than: very; extremely — before adjectives.
examples: I'd be *more than* happy to help.
The results were *more than* satisfactory.

senses.gloss: what's more: in addition, and this matters even more.
examples: The apartment is cheap, and *what's more*, it's close to work.
He was late again. *What's more*, he didn't apologize.

senses.gloss: no more than: only; not over.
examples: The drive takes *no more than* twenty minutes.
She was *no more than* a child when she left home.

position: before its word — before adjectives and adverbs (*most useful*); end after the verb (*what I miss most*)
modifies: verbs, adjectives, adverbs, and in informal American speech *every*, *all* and *everyone*
contrast: *The most* + adjective is the superlative (*the most interesting book* — самая интересная); *a most* + adjective, or *most* with nothing being compared (*That's most kind of you*), is formal and means *very* (*a most interesting book* — весьма интересная). Do not confuse the adverb with *mostly* (mainly): *What I like most is the food* vs *The audience was mostly students*. *Most people* (большинство людей) is the determiner; in that meaning it is never *most of people* (only *most of the people*), and *the most people* means 'the largest number of people'. *Most* meaning *almost* (*most everyone*) is informal American — avoid it in writing. One-syllable words take *-est*: *fastest*, never *most fast*.

senses.gloss: Used before adjectives and adverbs to form the superlative.
examples: It's the *most* beautiful park in the city.
Of all the drivers, she drove *most* carefully.
Which of these plans is *most* likely to work?

senses.gloss: To the greatest degree; more than anything else — with verbs.
examples: What I miss *most* is my mom's cooking.
The people who need help the *most* are often the last to ask for it.
*Most of all*, I want to thank my parents.

senses.gloss: at most, at the most: not more than; at the maximum.
examples: The drive takes an hour *at most*.
There were twenty people there, thirty *at the most*.
I can stay a week *at most*.

senses.gloss: Very; extremely — formal, often after *a*.
examples: That's *most* kind of you.
It was a *most* unusual evening.

senses.gloss: Almost — before *every*, *all*, *everyone* and *anyone*; informal American.
examples: *Most* everyone in town came to the game.
We eat there *most* every Friday.

position: before its word — before adjectives and adverbs (*less expensive*); end after the verb (*I worry less now*)
contrast: Everyday speech prefers *not as ... as* to *less* with short adjectives: *He's not as tall as his brother* sounds natural, *He's less tall than his brother* does not — and Russian *менее* before an adjective is often best translated that way. *Less* before a plural noun (*less people*) is a determiner use that careful writing replaces with *fewer*. *Less than happy* is a polite way to say *unhappy*, not a comparison. *Lesser* is an adjective (*the lesser evil*), not a comparative adverb.

senses.gloss: Used before adjectives and adverbs: not as; to a smaller degree.
examples: The second hotel was *less* expensive.
I see her *less* often now that she's moved.
The trail is *less* crowded on weekdays.

senses.gloss: To a smaller degree; a smaller amount — with verbs.
examples: Try to worry *less* and sleep more.
I've been driving *less and less* since I started biking to work.
My new job pays *less*, but I'm much happier.

senses.gloss: less than: not at all; far from — a polite understatement before an adjective.
examples: She was *less than* thrilled with the news.
The service at the hotel was *less than* perfect.

senses.gloss: no less: used to stress that an amount is surprisingly large or a person surprisingly important.
senses.ru: не менее, целых, не кто иной, как
examples: The house sold for *no less* than three million dollars.
The award was presented by the governor, *no less*.

position: before its word — before adjectives and adverbs (*the least expensive*); mid or end with verbs (*when you least expect it*)
modifies: verbs, adjectives, adverbs, numbers and whole clauses (*at least*)
contrast: Do not mix up *at least* (по крайней мере, хотя бы) and *at last* (наконец): *At last you're here!* is relief after waiting. *At least* before a number means 'no fewer than', and after a complaint it means 'still, one good thing is': *At least nobody got hurt*. *Not in the least* (ничуть) is emphatic and a little formal. *The least* before a noun (*the least money*) is the determiner and belongs to that dictionary.

senses.gloss: at least: not less than; at the minimum.
examples: The drive takes *at least* four hours.
You should brush your teeth *at least* twice a day.

senses.gloss: at least: anyway; even if nothing else is true or is done.
examples: The food was bad, but *at least* it was cheap.
You could *at least* call if you're going to be late.

senses.gloss: at least: or to put it more exactly — used to correct or limit what you have just said.
senses.ru: во всяком случае, по крайней мере
examples: She's coming to the party — *at least*, she said she was.
Nobody saw anything, or *at least* nobody's saying so.

senses.gloss: Used before adjectives and adverbs: to the smallest degree.
examples: This is the *least* expensive hotel in the area.
Math is the subject I'm *least* interested in.

senses.gloss: To the smallest degree; less than anything else — with verbs, and in *least of all*.
examples: Trouble always comes when you *least* expect it.
Nobody wanted to move, *least of all* my kids.

senses.gloss: not in the least: not at all.
examples: I'm not *in the least* surprised.
She didn't seem *in the least* worried about the exam.

position: end — after the verb (*We walked farther*); before its word with *away*, *down*, *north* and similar words (*farther down the road*)
modifies: verbs, and adverbs and prepositions of place (*farther away*, *farther from*)
contrast: Careful American usage keeps *farther* for physical distance and *further* for degree and addition: *We drove farther*, but *Let's discuss it further*. In speech *further* is used for distance too, but *farther* never means 'more' or 'in addition' — *Farther, the report found...* is wrong. Never *farer* or *more far*. *The farther shore* is the adjective.

senses.gloss: At or to a greater distance in space.
examples: I can't walk any *farther*.
Their house is a little *farther* down the road.
The *farther* north you go, the colder it gets.

senses.gloss: At or to a more distant point in time, or to a greater extent.
examples: We can trace the family *farther* back than 1800.
Nothing could be *farther* from the truth.

position: end — after the verb (*Who lives farthest?*)
modifies: verbs, and adverbs and prepositions of place (*farthest away*, *farthest from*)
contrast: Careful American usage keeps *farthest* for physical distance and prefers *furthest* for degree: *She lives farthest from school*, but *His proposal goes furthest toward fixing the problem*. Never *farest* or *most far*.

senses.gloss: At or to the greatest distance in space or time.
examples: Let's see who can throw the ball *farthest*.
The kids who live *farthest* from school take the bus.
This is the *farthest* north I've ever been.

position: end — after the verb and its object (*discuss it further*); front as a linker (*Further, the study found...*)
modifies: verbs, whole clauses, and adverbs and prepositions of place (*further down*)
contrast: *Further* covers everything *farther* does and more: only *further* means 'to a greater degree' (*Prices fell further*) or 'in addition' (*Further, the report found...*), though careful American writing still gives physical distance to *farther*. *Further* is also an adjective (*further information* — дополнительная информация) and a verb (*to further your career* — продвигать), both in other dictionaries; the linker *furthermore* is its own word. Russian *и так далее* is *and so on*, not *and so further*.

senses.gloss: To a greater degree or extent; more.
examples: We need to look into this *further*.
Prices dropped *further* in March.
I don't want to discuss it any *further*.

senses.gloss: At or to a greater distance in space or time, or later in a text.
examples: The gas station is a mile *further* down the road.
Let's walk a little *further* before we turn back.
See the chart *further* down the page.

senses.gloss: In addition; moreover — at the start of a sentence, formal.
examples: *Further*, the study found no link between the two.
The plan is expensive. *Further*, it would take years to finish.

position: end — after the verb (*Who traveled furthest?*)
modifies: verbs, and adverbs and prepositions of place (*furthest away*, *furthest from*)
contrast: Careful American writing uses *farthest* for physical distance, but *furthest* is common for distance in speech and is the only choice for degree: *the country that has gone furthest in cutting emissions*. *The furthest point* before a noun is the adjective.

senses.gloss: At or to the greatest distance in space or time.
examples: Of the three of us, I live *furthest* from the office.
The *furthest* back I can remember is our old house in Ohio.

senses.gloss: To the greatest degree or extent.
examples: Of all the candidates, she has gone *furthest* in promising tax cuts.
California has pushed *furthest* toward banning gas-powered cars.
